name: Thistle
lede: Thistle is a very pale, soft purple, one of the 140 named colors of the X11 set; the books say little about it, and what they say is mostly about the plant.

sections.title: A plant name, a screen color
sections.body: Paterson defines thistle as a purple colour, and gives the X11 Thistle as a very pale purple with the hex code #D8BFD8, a member of the 140-name X11 set [1]. In the dictionary's index it sits among the purples and pinks beside [[lilac]]-like names [1]. Our name data traces the swatch to the 1930 Maerz and Paul list and the 1955 ISCC-NBS system [2]. No book in our set explains why a thistle was chosen; the name simply points to the purple bloom of the plant, and the swatch is a pale tint of it.

sections.title: The plant in the dye vat
sections.body:
Thistles turn up in the dyer's story more than in the painter's. Safflower, a hardy thorned plant resembling a thistle, gave dyers reds and yellows that leaned toward orange or pink, and the pigment literature lists thistle saffron among the alternate names of the dye plant, a sign of historical confusion with true saffron [3][4]. For cheap local dyeing, Pastoureau notes, the leaves of thistle or parsley were among the ingredients used for yellows [3]. Balfour-Paul adds that woad farmers sometimes bulked their woad balls with thistles and other weeds [5].

None of these makes a purple. The color named thistle comes from the flower, not from the dye vat.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Thistle is rare in paintings: it appears in 0.03% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 8 paintings, as photographed, rarer than 73% of the named colors [6]. The earliest match is 1641, in a work by Alonso Cano, 289 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, so it is a look-alike hue and not proof of a pigment [6]. In printed English the adjective *thistle* peaks in the 1870s, and rose fastest in the 1820s [6]. For neighbors in the same quiet family, see [[mauve]], [[orchid]] and [[wisteria]].
